2026-11-01T08:14:02Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: No single bank point covers both hydroxide and carbonate neutralisation with the antacid example at Year 11 depth; the closest card covers only bases and adds Year 12 enthalpy and pH content, so a new point is safer.

draft.title: Neutralisation
card: Neutralisation is a reaction in which an acid reacts with a base and the acidic properties are used up. The products include a salt, which is an ionic compound made from the acid's negative ion and the base's positive ion.
makes a salt and water. For example, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O.
makes a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. For example, 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The gas makes bubbles.
Antacid tablets contain bases such as magnesium hydroxide or calcium carbonate. They neutralise some of the excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
draft.remember: Acid + hydroxide gives salt + water. Acid + carbonate also gives carbon dioxide.

a.q: Sulfuric acid reacts completely with sodium hydroxide solution. Which products form?
opts: Sodium sulfate, water and carbon dioxide
a.why: An acid and a hydroxide form a salt and water. The salt is sodium sulfate. Carbon dioxide only forms when the base is a carbonate, and no carbonate is present here.
a.clue: The base here is a hydroxide, not a carbonate.

b.q: Ravi takes an antacid tablet containing calcium carbonate for excess stomach acid. Which products form in the stomach?
opts: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide
Calcium chloride, water and hydrogen gas
b.why: Stomach acid is hydrochloric acid. With a carbonate it forms a salt (calcium chloride), water and carbon dioxide. The tempting answer of calcium chloride and water only would be right for a hydroxide, but this base is a carbonate.
b.clue: Check whether the base is a hydroxide or a carbonate.

b.best: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide
